sections.title: Deeper Understanding of Statement and Assumption
sections.content: At Level 2, identifying the hidden idea behind a statement requires deeper thinking. A statement often describes a decision, plan, or strategy. An assumption is the underlying belief that the speaker considers to be true. If this underlying belief turns out to be incorrect, the entire statement may become weak.

sections.title: Difference Between Valid Assumption and Future Consequence
sections.content: A valid assumption is something that must be true for the statement to make sense. A future consequence is a result that may happen later. In exams, options often present consequences as if they were assumptions. Therefore, it is important to identify which idea is already believed to be true and which idea might happen later.

sections.title: Policy Implementation Assumptions
sections.content: When a government or institution introduces a major policy or scheme, it is assumed that the necessary resources exist to implement it. These resources may include funds, manpower, technology, or infrastructure. Without these basic requirements, the plan cannot succeed.

sections.title: Corporate Strategy Assumptions
sections.content: Companies often adopt new strategies such as launching a product or implementing a new HR policy. In such situations, it is assumed that the decision will improve productivity or increase market share and will not negatively affect employees or customers.

sections.title: Identifying Invalid Assumptions
sections.content: Some options are not assumptions but merely guesses or conclusions. Invalid assumptions usually fall into three categories: ideas that are too broad, ideas that are not factually related to the statement, or results that may occur in the future but are not necessary for the statement.

sections.title: 3–4 Step Logical Evaluation Method
sections.content: Step 1: Read the statement carefully and understand its objective. Step 2: Identify the hidden belief that the speaker is relying on. Step 3: Reverse the option and check whether the statement becomes weak. Step 4: Ensure the option is a prior belief rather than a future outcome.

sections.title: Difference Between Assumption and Inference
sections.content: An assumption is the foundation on which the statement is based. An inference is a conclusion that can be drawn after reading the statement. Exams often include inference-type options as assumptions to confuse students.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Treating possible results as assumptions. 2. Choosing overly broad or general options. 3. Selecting information already given in the statement as an assumption. 4. Ignoring the purpose of the statement while selecting the answer.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: At Level 2, identifying assumptions requires understanding which idea forms the necessary base of the statement. In policy or corporate strategy questions, assumptions often relate to resources, human behavior, and expected impact.

tricks.title: Base Requirement Trick
tricks.explanation: If a statement discusses a plan or strategy, the assumption often relates to the required resources.
tricks.example: Statement: The government launched free internet across the country. Assumption: Adequate technical infrastructure is available.

tricks.title: Future Result Trap Trick
tricks.explanation: If an option describes a future outcome, it is usually a consequence, not an assumption.
tricks.example: Statement: The company launched a new product. Option: The company's profits will definitely increase. This is a possible result, not an assumption.

tricks.title: Corporate Strategy Identification
tricks.explanation: Corporate decisions usually assume that the new action will have a positive impact.
tricks.example: Statement: The company introduced a flexible working policy. Assumption: Employee productivity will not decrease.

tricks.title: Infrastructure Check Trick
tricks.explanation: Large-scale plans assume the presence of required infrastructure.
tricks.example: Statement: The government announced digital education in every village. Assumption: Villages may have access to internet or devices.

tricks.title: Over-Generalization Trap
tricks.explanation: Options making extremely broad claims are usually incorrect assumptions.
tricks.example: Statement: A new bus service started in the city. Option: Everyone will prefer traveling by bus. This is overly broad.

tricks.title: Negative Test Method
tricks.explanation: Reverse the assumption. If the statement collapses, the assumption is correct.
tricks.example: Statement: The company reduced prices. Assumption: Lower prices attract customers.

tricks.title: Hidden Premise Identification
tricks.explanation: The hidden connection between the action and its intended purpose is the assumption.
tricks.example: Statement: The school started online classes. Assumption: Students have access to the internet.

tricks.title: Inference Trap
tricks.explanation: If an option is a conclusion drawn from the statement, it is not an assumption.
tricks.example: Statement: The company increased production. Option: Demand for the product is very high. This is an inference.

tricks.title: Decision Support Trick
tricks.explanation: An assumption often provides the logical support for the decision mentioned in the statement.
tricks.example: Statement: The college built a new library. Assumption: Students need additional study resources.

tricks.title: Direct Relevance Rule
tricks.explanation: The correct assumption must be directly connected to the purpose of the statement.
tricks.example: Statement: Bicycle tracks were built in the city. Assumption: Some people want to travel by bicycle.
